newsitem.title: PERU: Peru court reaches Fujimori re-election decision.
newsitem.headline: Peru court reaches Fujimori re-election decision.

text.p: Peru's highest court for constitutional matters decided on Friday whether to allow President Alberto Fujimori to run for a third term -- but postponed announcing its verdict until the hostage crisis ends.

"The members of this tribunal have unanimously decided to suspend the publication of the sentence ... until the emergency has passed," Delia Revoredo, one of the Constitutional Court's seven magistrates, told reporters.
Local media have speculated in recent days the court has overruled Congress' previous decision to allow Fujimori to run for a third term in 2000.
Such a decision would mean Fujimori would have to rewrite the constitution if, as is widely believed, he wanted to try and maintain power into the next century.

But Revoredo said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima meant it was impossible to announce the decision on Friday as previously scheduled.

"We believe the country and the government are passing through a very difficult and delicate situation, and we want to contribute with the most suitable atmosphere for President Fujimori and the government to conclude this negotiation in the best way possible," she said.
"We believe our sentence is so important and delicate that it could cause political reactions that would not help this situation."
Under Peruvian law a president who has been elected for two consecutive terms, as has Fujimori, cannot run in the following election.
But Congress voted in August in favour of a legal interpretation that meant Fujimori's first term would not be taken into account should he wish to stand for reelection.

Fujimori was elected president in 1990 and again in 1995 with 64 percent of the vote. After he dissolved parliament during his 1992 "self-coup," a new constitution was written the following year by a reformulated Congress, paving the way for the interpretation accepted in August.

Speculation about the Constitutional Court's decision came as Fujimori faced the toughest test of his six years in office, with Marxist rebels holding 74 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima for the 17th day.
The president has not formally announced an intention to run again in 2000, but has been quoted off the record by some close sources as saying that he wants to.
